---
title: "Case Study: Bill Walsh's 49ers and the West Coast Offense"
subtitle: "How a team that couldn't yet run the ball made the short pass its running game, and how its coaches spread across the league."
description: "A Level 4 case study of Bill Walsh's San Francisco 49ers (1979–1988) and the West Coast offense: the problem Walsh inherited, the horizontal passing game as a substitute for the run, timing, yards after the catch and ball placement as design goals, scripting and Walsh's practice methods, a frame-by-frame breakdown of 'The Catch' (Sprint Right Option, 1981 NFC Championship), the data fingerprint of short passing in today's NFL, how defenses answered, the Walsh coaching tree (with the 2025 and 2026 head coaches labelled separately), and what survives."
glossary:
  "Horizontal passing game": "An offense built on short, timed throws toward the sidelines and across the field, caught a few yards past the line of scrimmage and turned into gains by the run after the catch. It uses the pass to do the running game's job (gain four or five yards, keep the ball, stretch the defense from side to side), which is why its throws are often called extended handoffs. Bill Walsh's 49ers made it the core of the West Coast offense."
  "Coaching tree": "The family of coaches descended from one head coach, traced through who worked on whose staff: a branch runs from a head coach or coordinator to an assistant who later led a staff of his own. Because most coaches work for several bosses, one coach can sit on several branches. A tree records where coaches learned, not that they run the same plays."

#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"
#| output: false
import logging
logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, RegularPolygon
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, technique, style, routes as r

style.apply()
GREEN = "#0f7a55"          # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
OL_KEYS = ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


def O(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line():
    """The five offensive linemen with one-letter labels, T G C G T."""
    short = {"LT": "T", "LG": "G", "C": "C", "RG": "G", "RT": "T"}
    return [p.moved(label=short[p.key]) for p in offense("singleback") if p.key in OL_KEYS]


def T(t, side=1):
    """Width of technique t on the offense's right (side=+1) or left (side=-1)."""
    return technique(t, side)


def split_backs(y_side=1, z_w=13.0, x_w=-13.0, h_side=-1):
    """Walsh's base look: split backs (the pro set), one back behind each tackle, a tight end, a split end (X)
    and a flanker (Z). The halfback (H) is on the offense's left by default; h_side=+1 puts him on the right."""
    return line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("HB", "RB", -5.0, 3.2 * h_side, "H"),
                     O("FB", "FB", -5.0, -3.2 * h_side, "F"),
                     O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8 * y_side, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, x_w, "X"),
                     O("Z", "WR", -1.5, z_w, "Z")]


def era_43(shell="one", ss_side=1):
    """A 1980s 4-3 Over against a pro set (tight end on the offense's right), corners 7 off."""
    dfn = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "E"), D("WT", "DT", 1.0, T("1", -1), "T"),
           D("ST", "DT", 1.0, T("3"), "T"), D("SE", "DE", 1.0, T("5") + 0.2, "E"),
           D("SAM", "LB", 4.0, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.5, 0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.5, -3.0, "W"),
           D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -13.5, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 13.5, "CB")]
    if shell == "two":
        dfn += [D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 8.0, "SS")]
    else:
        dfn += [D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 8.0, 7.5 * ss_side, "SS")]
    return dfn


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, pull, path, run, rush or route."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "pull":
        return p.pull(key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "rush":
        return p.rush(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "route":
        return p.route(key, [tuple(q) for q in (*via, end)], absolute=True, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def pass_pro(p, keys=OL_KEYS, depth=-1.2):
    for k in keys:
        p.block(k, pts=[(depth + 0.7, 0.0)])


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.2, ha="center", weight="normal", alpha=0.92):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9,
                fontweight=weight, clip_on=True,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=alpha))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, shrink=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92))


def num(fld, p, d, w, n, color=GREEN):
    """A numbered progression circle."""
    x, y = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, d, w))
    fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.85, fc="white", ec=color, lw=1.4, zorder=10))
    fld.ax.text(x, y, str(n), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7, color=color, fontweight="bold", zorder=11)


def clean(ax, numbers=True):
    """Drop hash ticks (and optionally yard numbers); clip text to the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if numbers and t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=6.2, ax=None, numbers=True, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page, cleaned for a zoomed window."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax, numbers=numbers)
    return fld


def ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15), fs=6.5):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) along the left edge of the window."""
    x_left = (160 / 3) - fld.y1 + 0.4
    for d in depths:
        y = p.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 0.8 <= y <= fld.x1 - 0.8:
            fld.ax.text(x_left, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == depths[0] else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                        ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def title(ax, text, size=8.6):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=size, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


# --- frame strips (PDF) and video (web) for simulated plays ------------------------------------------
MARK_R = 0.62


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def catch_time(df, key, t_throw):
    """First tracking time after the throw when the ball reaches `key` (the simulated catch)."""
    b = df[df.side == "ball"].set_index("time")[["x", "y"]]
    q = df[df.displayName == key].set_index("time")[["x", "y"]]
    gap = ((b - q) ** 2).sum(axis=1) ** 0.5
    gap = gap[gap.index > t_throw + 0.05]
    return float(gap[gap < 0.6].index[0])


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=(), ring_r=0.95, mark_r=None, trails=None):
    """One moment of a simulated play on `ax`: markers, trails (only for the keys in `trails`, if given), rings."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.5, play.los + window[1] - 0.3)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.5, yhi - 0.5) | (cur["side"] == "ball")]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    keep = ids if trails is None else ids & set(trails)
    tr = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(keep) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in tr.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    mr = mark_r or MARK_R
    for _, r_ in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r_["x"], r_["y"]))
        if r_["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.45), 0.75, 0.45, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=12))
            continue
        lab = str(r_.get("label", "") or "")
        if r_["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), mr, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=mr * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * mr / MARK_R * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.6)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        r_ = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r_["x"], r_["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), ring_r, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.6, zorder=7))
    for patch in ax.patches:
        patch.set_clip_on(True)
    return fld


def strip(moments, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), ncols=2, width_in=6.2, after=None, mark_r=None,
          trails=None, note_h=0.8):
    """Numbered frame strip. `moments` is a list of (play, t, tag)."""
    cache = {}
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(moments) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (note_h if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(moments):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, (play, t, tag)) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, moments)):
        if id(play) not in cache:
            cache[id(play)] = tracking(play)
        fld = panel(ax, play, cache[id(play)], t, lateral, window, rings, mark_r=mark_r, trails=trails)
        if after:
            after(fld, play, t, i)
        lab = "snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  {lab}" + (f"   {tag}" if tag else ""), fontsize=8.3, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                    fontsize=7.1 if ncols < 3 else 6.6, color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.3 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(play, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), width_in=4.8, after=None, mark_r=None, trails=None):
    """Web version: the play frame by frame, with each moment's note shown as the caption."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.5))
    df = tracking(play)
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    frames = [float(tmap[f]) for f in sorted(df["frameId"].unique())]

    def update(k):
        t = frames[k]
        ax.clear()
        fld = panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings, mark_r=mark_r, trails=trails)
        if after:
            after(fld, play, t, -1)
        cur = [n for tt, n in notes if tt <= t + 1e-6]
        ax.set_title(("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s") + (("\n" + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""),
                     fontsize=8.2, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=range(len(frames)), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animation_or_strip(play, moments, lateral, window, rings=(), after=None, ncols=2, width_in=6.2, mark_r=None,
                       trails=None, note_h=0.8):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF. moments = [(t, tag, note)]."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip([(play, t, tag) for t, tag, _ in moments], lateral, window, notes=[n for *_, n in moments],
              rings=rings, ncols=ncols, width_in=width_in, after=after, mark_r=mark_r, trails=trails, note_h=note_h)
        plt.show()
        return
    video(play, [(t, n) for t, _, n in moments], lateral, window, rings=rings, after=after, mark_r=mark_r,
          trails=trails)
```

#| code-summary: "Show the Python (the data: early-down runs and passes, 2023-2025)"
# Every early-down snap in a competitive game, 2023-2025 regular seasons, from nflverse play-by-play.
from gridiron.data import pbp

COLS = ["season", "season_type", "posteam", "down", "qtr", "wp", "play_type", "air_yards", "complete_pass",
        "yards_after_catch", "receiving_yards", "yards_gained", "epa", "success", "qb_spike", "qb_kneel",
        "qb_scramble", "qb_dropback", "sack"]
raw = pbp([2023, 2024, 2025], columns=COLS)
ED = raw[(raw.season_type == "REG") & raw.down.isin([1, 2]) & raw.wp.between(0.10, 0.90)
         & (raw.qb_spike != 1) & (raw.qb_kneel != 1)]
RUNS = ED[(ED.play_type == "run") & (ED.qb_scramble != 1)]
PASSES = ED[(ED.play_type == "pass") & ED.air_yards.notna()]          # thrown balls (sacks have no air yards)
DROPBACKS = ED[ED.qb_dropback == 1]                                    # passes + sacks + scrambles
BINS = [(-99, 0, "Pass, thrown behind\nthe line (screens, swings)"), (0, 5, "Pass, 1–5 yards\nin the air"),
        (5, 10, "Pass, 6–10 yards"), (10, 15, "Pass, 11–15 yards"), (15, 99, "Pass, 16+ yards")]


def summary(df):
    return pd.Series({"n": len(df), "sr": df.success.mean(), "epa": df.epa.mean(), "yds": df.yards_gained.mean()})


ROWS = [("Designed run", summary(RUNS))]
for lo, hi, lab in BINS:
    ROWS.append((lab, summary(PASSES[(PASSES.air_yards > lo) & (PASSES.air_yards <= hi)])))
ROWS.append(("Every dropback\n(sacks and scrambles in)", summary(DROPBACKS)))
TAB = pd.DataFrame({lab: s for lab, s in ROWS}).T
N_PASS = len(PASSES)
SHORT = PASSES[PASSES.air_yards <= 5]
SHORT_SHARE = len(SHORT) / N_PASS
BEHIND_SHARE = (PASSES.air_yards <= 0).mean()
RUN_SR, RUN_YDS = TAB.loc["Designed run", "sr"], TAB.loc["Designed run", "yds"]
S15 = TAB.iloc[2]
SCR = TAB.iloc[1]
_c15 = PASSES[(PASSES.air_yards > 0) & (PASSES.air_yards <= 5) & (PASSES.complete_pass == 1)]
YAC_SHORT = _c15.yards_after_catch.sum() / _c15.receiving_yards.sum()

# the 2025 census benchmark: early-down throws of 5 air yards or less, by team
P25 = PASSES[PASSES.season == 2025]
TEAM25 = P25.groupby("posteam").air_yards.apply(lambda s: (s <= 5).mean()).sort_values()
LG25 = (P25.air_yards <= 5).mean()
# do the Walsh-tree teams of 2025 (their head coaches are in the tree figure) throw short more than the rest?
TREE25 = ["KC", "SF", "LA", "GB", "MIN", "CIN", "JAX", "BAL", "MIA", "CLE"]
TREE_SH = P25[P25.posteam.isin(TREE25)].air_yards.le(5).mean()
REST_SH = P25[~P25.posteam.isin(TREE25)].air_yards.le(5).mean()
JAX_RANK = int(TEAM25.rank(ascending=False)["JAX"])


def ordinal(n):
    return f"{n}{'th' if 10 <= n % 100 <= 20 else {1: 'st', 2: 'nd', 3: 'rd'}.get(n % 10, 'th')}"

#set figure(placement: auto)
```

Third-and-3 at the Dallas 6, fifty-eight seconds left in the 1981 NFC Championship Game, the 49ers
behind 27–21. Joe Montana takes the snap and sprints to his right with three Cowboys chasing him
toward the sideline. His first receiver has slipped. Montana pump-fakes, backpedals, and throws the
ball high toward the back of the end zone, so high that the Cowboys' defensive end Ed "Too Tall" Jones,
who had left his feet on the fake, can't reach it. Dwight Clark jumps and gets his fingertips to it.
It's the most famous catch in the sport, and it gets called a miracle, a desperation heave, a throwaway
that a receiver happened to catch. Clark always said it was none of those things: it was a play from the
book, run on the practice field so many times that he knew where the ball would be.[^catch] Which was
it? And how did a team that had gone 2–14 two years earlier end up in that spot at all? The answers are
the same answer, and it's the subject of this chapter.

**You'll be able to:**

- Explain how Walsh's **horizontal passing game** works as a substitute for the run, and say what it
  costs: why a five-yard throw can do a handoff's job and when it can't.
- Explain timing, yards after the catch and ball placement as *design goals*, built into every route
  and every drop, and spot each one on a broadcast replay.
- Describe how Walsh scripted games and ran practice, and explain why a timing offense depends on
  rehearsal more than a run-first one does.
- Break down "The Catch" (the 1981 NFC Championship) step by step: the call, the design, what went
  wrong, and why the play still worked.
- Trace the Walsh **coaching tree** from his assistants to the head coaches of the 2025 and 2026
  seasons, and say what a tree does and doesn't tell you.
- Run a "West Coast census" on a modern game: count the short horizontal throws on early downs, and
  compare them with the league's numbers.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
This is a Level 4 case study, and it builds on two chapters in particular. One line each:

- **[1978 and the Passing Revolution](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd)**: two 1978 rules
  (the [Mel Blount rule](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mel-blount-rule-1978) and open-hand pass
  blocking) freed receivers past five yards and gave quarterbacks time; Coryell answered by stretching
  the field deep, Walsh by stretching it sideways.
- **[Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)**: a
  [pass concept](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pass-concept) is a set of routes built to put one
  defender in a bind, read in a numbered order. You'll see [drive](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-drive-concept)
  (a shallow cross under a dig) and the [curl-flat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat)
  triangle again here.

Terms from elsewhere you'll meet often: the [West Coast offense](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-west-coast-offense)
([WCO](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-wco)) and its long play calls, from
[Offensive Systems](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd);
[slant](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slant), [flat route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flat-route),
[timing route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-timing-route),
[progression](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-progression),
[YAC](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-yac) (yards after the catch) and the
[horizontal stretch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horizontal-stretch), from
[Passing Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd);
[slant-flat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slant-flat) and the
[rhythm throw](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rhythm-throw), from
[The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd); the
[pro set](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pro-set), also called
[split backs](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-split-backs), from
[Classic Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd);
[check-release](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-check-release), from
[Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd);
[Cover 3](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-3), from
[The Cover 3 Family](../06-pass-coverage/06-03-cover-3-family.qmd); the
[opening script](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-opening-script), from
[The Game Plan](../08-the-chess-match/08-03-game-planning-week.qmd); and
[EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa) and
[success rate](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-success-rate), from
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd).

*Reading the diagrams:* offense is blue circles (Q quarterback; H the halfback and F the fullback in
split backs; X, Y, Z the receivers, Y the tight end; T G C G T the line). Defense is outlined squares
(E end, T tackle, S M W the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, CB corners, FS and SS safeties). Solid
arrows are routes and runs, a thick dark arrow is the ball carrier, dashed orange arrows are defenders'
drops, a bar at the end of a line is a block, and the dashed brown line is the pass. A green ring marks
the player to watch; numbered green circles are the quarterback's progression. The left-edge numbers
give depth in yards past the line of scrimmage. Plays are illustrative, typical of the era, not traced
from film, unless a caption says otherwise.
:::

## The problem: 2–14, and no way to run the ball

In January 1979 the San Francisco 49ers hired a 47-year-old Stanford coach to fix a franchise that
had just gone 2–14. Bill Walsh had waited a long time for the job. He had coached in pro football since
1966, with the Raiders (then an AFL team) and then for eight seasons with Paul Brown's Cincinnati Bengals, where he ran the
passing game. When Brown retired from coaching after the 1975 season he picked another assistant, Bill
"Tiger" Johnson, as his successor; Walsh resigned, and later said Brown had worked against him when
other teams asked about him for head-coaching jobs. He spent 1976 as the Chargers' offensive
coordinator, coaching a young Dan Fouts, and two seasons winning at Stanford before the 49ers called.
He was also the general manager, which mattered: the man drawing the plays was the man choosing the
players.[^walshbio]

What he inherited was a team with no good answer to the oldest question in football: how do you keep
the ball? In the 1970s the answer was the run. A team that could gain four yards on first down and four
more on second down controlled the clock, the field and the game, and passing was what you did when that
failed. Walsh's 49ers couldn't do it. They didn't have the linemen to push other teams around, and
Walsh had been in exactly this spot before. Of the young expansion Bengals he had coached in the late
1960s, he said: "We couldn't control the football with the run; teams were just too strong. So it had
to be the forward pass, and obviously it had to be a high-percentage, short, controlled passing
game."[^quote]

That sentence is the whole chapter in miniature. Walsh didn't decide to *pass more* instead of running.
He decided that the pass could *be* his running game, doing the same job (four yards at a time, the
clock moving, the ball kept) with players and plays he could actually win with. He had already proved
it once, with Virgil Carter in Cincinnati (the story is in
[The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd)); San Francisco let him build a whole team
around it, just after the 1978 rules had made it far easier.

You've met the outline of this story in [1978 and the Passing Revolution](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd):
the hire, Montana in the third round of the 1979 draft (with Dwight Clark in the tenth), 2–14 and then
6–10, and Super Bowl XVI two years later.[^draft] This chapter is the version with the clock running:
what the plays looked like snap by snap, why each piece was there, and what happened to the system
after its inventor left.

## The scheme answer: the pass as a run

Here is the idea in one term. A [**horizontal passing game**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horizontal-passing-game)
is an offense built on short, timed throws toward the sidelines and across the field, caught a few yards
past the line of scrimmage and turned into gains by the run after the catch. Its throws are so short that
they're often described as extended handoffs.[^quote2] The name contrasts it with the *vertical* passing
of Don Coryell's Chargers, which attacked down the field.

What does a run actually do for an offense? Three things. It gains a few yards with little risk of
losing many. It puts the ball in a fast player's hands while he's moving forward, so he can make a
defender miss. And it attacks the defense at a spot the offense chose. A short pass to the flat does all
three, and @fig-same-job shows the comparison that Walsh's offense made every week: two ways to get the
halfback to the right edge with the ball.

```{python}
#| label: fig-same-job
#| fig-cap: "The same job, two ways (illustrative, 1980s 4-3, Cover 3). Left: a toss sweep. The halfback (H, green ring) needs four blockers (grey rings) to win at once: the right tackle and tight end reach their men, the right guard pulls around the tight end to lead on the strong safety, and the flanker (Z) blocks the cornerback. Even then the Mike linebacker, flowing over the top unblocked, can make the tackle; one lost block and it's a loss. Right: the halfback runs a flat route instead and the quarterback throws it on a three-step drop, so the ball arrives about a second and a half after the snap, near the sideline. The strong safety (SS) is the one defender responsible for both the tight end's curl and the flat, and he can't be in both places. Here he sinks under the curl, so the flat is the throw; if he had widened to the flat, the curl behind him would be. No one has to win a block at the edge. That is the horizontal passing game: a pass that does a run's job."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.3))
LAT, WIN = (-5.0, 21.5), (-8.0, 15.5)

# ---------------- left: toss sweep right
p = Play(split_backs(z_w=13.5, h_side=1), era_43("one"), los=35, to_go=10)
go_to(p, "HB", (3.0, 11.8), kind="run", via=[(-4.4, 5.6), (-2.0, 10.0)], speed=6.5)  # the halfback takes the toss
p.pitch("HB", t=0.45)
go_to(p, "FB", (-1.4, -4.4), kind="block", speed=4.0)                      # the fullback cuts off the backside end
go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 4.6), kind="block")                                   # reach the end
go_to(p, "Y", (2.2, 7.0), kind="block")                                    # reach the Sam
go_to(p, "RG", (2.0, 8.8), kind="pull", via=[(-1.6, 2.4), (-1.0, 6.6)])     # pull around Y, lead on the force
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(0.6, 0.6)])
go_to(p, "SAM", (2.6, 7.6), kind="path", speed=4.5)
go_to(p, "MIKE", (2.4, 6.0), kind="path", speed=4.5)                       # flows over the top, unblocked
go_to(p, "SS", (3.2, 10.4), kind="path", speed=4.5)
go_to(p, "Z", (4.6, 14.6), kind="block")                                     # Z blocks the corner
p.highlight("HB")
p.highlight("RT", "Y", "RG", "Z", color=style.INK_2)
fld = draw(p, ax=axes[0], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
title(axes[0], "A toss sweep: four blocks to win the edge")
say(fld, p, 9.8, 15.6, "the defense\nflows to it", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(fld, p, (6.0, 1.4), (2.4, 6.0), "M: unblocked", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
say(fld, p, -6.6, 13.4, "grey rings: 4 blockers\nwho must all win", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)

# ---------------- right: the flat pass
dfn = [q.moved(w=15.0) if q.key == "RCB" else q.moved(d=7.0, w=9.0) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in era_43("one")]
p = Play(split_backs(z_w=15.0, h_side=1), dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
p.dropback(3.2)
pass_pro(p)
p.block("FB", pts=[(0.3, -0.5)])
go_to(p, "HB", (0.8, 10.8), kind="route", via=[(-3.2, 6.2)])
go_to(p, "HB", (6.4, 12.2), kind="run", speed=6.2)
p.route("Y", r.curl(10))
p.route("Z", r.go(12))
p.drop("SS", (9.0, 6.2), speed=4.2)                                        # sinks under the curl...
p.drop("RCB", (13.0, 15.5))
go_to(p, "SAM", (4.6, 5.6), kind="path", speed=3.8)
p.pass_to("HB", t=1.0)
p.highlight("HB")
fld = draw(p, ax=axes[1], lateral=LAT, window=WIN, title=False)
title(axes[1], "A flat pass: the ball outruns the pursuit")
say(fld, p, -6.6, 9.2, "3-step drop:\nball out in ~1 s", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(fld, p, (-3.4, 12.8), (3.4, 11.5), "run after\nthe catch", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
point_to(fld, p, (12.6, 9.6), (9.0, 6.2), "SS: curl or flat?\nHe sinks", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
plt.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

Look at what the pass *removes*. The toss sweep is a bet that four blockers each win their fight in the
same second; the flat pass is a bet that one throw is accurate. Against a defense that's bigger and
stronger than your line, the second bet is the better one, and in 1979 the 49ers' line was the weak
point. The pass also changes *who* does the tackling. On a run the first defenders to arrive are linemen
and linebackers, the biggest men on the field. On a quick throw to the edge the tackler is usually a
defensive back, 30 or 40 pounds lighter, and often backing up when the ball arrives.

Then there is the [horizontal stretch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horizontal-stretch), which is
what makes the throw hard to take away. You can see it in the right panel: in this Cover 3 the strong
safety is the [curl-flat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat) defender, responsible for both
the tight end's curl and the flat, and two receivers are in his area at once. Whichever he takes, the
quarterback throws the other. A zone defender who covers the flat can't also cover a route breaking
inside him, so the offense puts a receiver on each side of him and throws to whichever he leaves. Spread that across the field (the backs releasing to both flats, receivers crossing underneath)
and every short defender has two receivers to worry about. The defense can't add enough players
underneath to cover them all without emptying the deep part of the field. That, Walsh argued, was when
the long throw came open.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists, and what it costs"}
The horizontal passing game exists because **a team that can't win at the line of scrimmage can still
win in space**. It trades the run's physical contest for a contest of precision and speed: the ball gets
to the edge before the defense does, and the tackle is made, or missed, by a smaller man in open field.

The bill comes in four parts. **It needs an accurate quarterback**, more than a strong-armed one: a
throw a yard behind the receiver turns a five-yard gain into a tackle at the catch. **It needs receivers
who run after the catch**, because the throw itself only travels a few yards. **A short throw can still
be intercepted**, and a linebacker who reads it and jumps it has a clear run the other way. And **it
gets squeezed**: once a defense stops worrying about the deep ball, its underneath defenders can crowd
the short throws, which is why Walsh insisted the offense keep threatening deep. A West Coast team
that only throws short isn't running Walsh's offense.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"The West Coast offense is dink-and-dunk."** Walsh hated the word *finesse*, which writers attached
to his offense, and the record supports him.[^finesse] The short throws were the setup, not the point: they
pulled linebackers and safeties forward, and the 49ers then threw over them. Jerry Rice caught 22
touchdown passes in twelve games in 1987, many of them long runs after slants and deep throws, which is
not what dink-and-dunk looks like.[^rice] What *is* true is that the offense was built so that a short
gain was an acceptable result, which most 1970s passing games couldn't say.
:::

**And the running game came back.** "Couldn't run" describes the 49ers Walsh inherited, not the team he
built. In 1979 they ran on 44% of their plays, against 54% for the league as a whole, and threw more
passes than any other team. By 1981 they ran on 52% (league: 51%), and in 1984 on 52% again (league:
49%), when Wendell Tyler set a team record with 1,262 rushing yards.[^runpass] The short passing game
didn't replace the run; it made the run possible again. Linebackers who had to respect two backs
releasing into routes, and safeties pulled forward by short throws, left fewer defenders to stop a
handoff. The run in turn gave the 49ers their
[play-action](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-play-action) passes: a fake to a back from split
backs, with the quarterback under center and his back to the defense, froze linebackers who had been
burned by both. That under-center play-action is the bridge to Mike Shanahan's offense, later in this
chapter.

## Design goal 1: timing

Walsh's offense is a timing offense, the purest version of the idea you met in
[Passing Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd): the quarterback's drop
and the receiver's route are designed as one unit, so that the ball leaves his hand at the moment the
receiver breaks, and arrives before the defender can react. That chapter's chart of drops and route
depths is the West Coast offense's skeleton: a three-step drop for quick routes caught about 5 to 7
yards downfield (a slant breaks after three hard steps, about 4 yards, and is caught at 6 or 7), a
five-step drop with a hitch for routes at 10 to 14, a seven-step drop for the deep comebacks and posts.

On a broadcast replay, a timed throw has a look you can learn. **The ball leaves the quarterback's hand
before the receiver has finished his break**, often before the receiver has turned his head, and the
receiver catches it without slowing down. A throw that waits until the receiver is visibly open, and
standing still, is a late throw, however good the result.

Two things made Walsh's version different from a generic timing game.

**The quarterback's feet were his reading clock.** Each step of the drop meant a receiver in the
progression. On the last step of a quick drop he threw to the first receiver if he was open. If not,
the hitch step that followed was his permission to go to the second, and so on down to the
[checkdown](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown). This is why the offense could be taught: a
quarterback didn't have to *decide* when to give up on a receiver, because his feet decided for him.

**The backs were receivers, not spare blockers.** The original West Coast offense lined up in
[split backs](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-split-backs): one back behind each tackle, a tight end,
and two wide receivers.[^wco] On a pass play both backs had rules that turned them into receivers. Each
checked his blocking assignment first (a linebacker who might blitz) and released into a short route if
nobody came, which is the [check-release](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-check-release). A defense that
covered all five possible receivers had to account for both backs, and a defense that blitzed found a
back already in its way.

When the blitz brought more rushers than the backs and line could block, the answer was the same as in
any dropback offense: a [hot route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hot-route), a receiver (often
the tight end or the back on the blitz side) who knows to look for the ball immediately, and a
[sight adjustment](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sight-adjust) by a wide receiver who converts his
route into a quick slant when he sees the blitz. The quick throw goes where the blitzer came from.
(The protection side of this is in [Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd).)

[The 1978 chapter](../11-history/11-02-the-1978-liberation.qmd) drew the slant side of Walsh's most
basic read: the Will linebacker widens to the flat, and the ball goes to the slant inside him.
@fig-slant-flat-strip is the other half of the same read, with the clock running: the
[slant-flat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slant-flat) from split backs, the Will sinking under the
slant, and the ball going to the halfback in the flat.

```{python}
#| label: fig-slant-flat-strip
#| fig-cap: "Slant-flat from split backs, with the halfback in the flat (simulated, BDB-format tracking; illustrative 1980s 4-3, Cover 3). The quarterback takes three steps from under center. X runs a slant, three hard steps and then the break inside; the halfback (H, ringed) checks for a blitzer, then releases to the flat. The Will (W, ringed) is the one defender between them, and here he sinks inside under the slant, so the throw goes to H. It leaves the quarterback's hand about 1.3 seconds after the snap, before H has reached the flat. H catches it on the run near the numbers, about three yards past the line, a little over two seconds after the snap, and turns up the sideline for five or six more yards before the cornerback, who had backed up to guard his deep third, can come back down. Faint lines are where each player has been; the brown dot is the ball."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
sf = Play(split_backs(), era_43("one"), los=35, to_go=10)
sf.dropback(3.2)
pass_pro(sf)
sf.block("FB", pts=[(0.4, -0.6)])
sf.route("X", [(0, 0), (4.0, 0), (8.4, -5.6)], speed=6.8)                     # slant: 3 hard steps, then break
go_to(sf, "HB", (3.0, -13.0), kind="route", via=[(-3.4, -6.0), (-0.4, -10.0)], delay=0.3,
      speed=7.0)                                                               # check for a blitzer, then the flat
go_to(sf, "HB", (8.8, -16.0), kind="run", speed=6.4)                         # run after the catch
sf.route("Y", r.curl(10))
sf.route("Z", r.go(10))
go_to(sf, "WILL", (5.4, -5.0), kind="path", speed=4.3)                      # Will sinks under the slant
go_to(sf, "LCB", (11.4, -14.2), kind="path", speed=4.0)                      # corner bails, deep third
go_to(sf, "LCB", (10.6, -14.6), kind="path", delay=0.15, speed=3.0)          # then breaks down
go_to(sf, "MIKE", (7.2, -1.0), kind="path", speed=4.0)
go_to(sf, "FS", (16.0, 0.0), kind="path", speed=3.0)
sf.pass_to("HB", t=1.3)
SF_CATCH = catch_time(tracking(sf), "HB", 1.3)

SF_NOTES = ["Split backs, three-step drop.\nWill (W) is the one man between\nthe slant (X) and the flat (H).",
            "Third step lands, about 1.3 s. W\nsinks under the slant, so the ball\ngoes to H, who isn't there yet.",
            "H catches it in stride near\nthe numbers, already running,\nabout three yards past the line.",
            "Run after the catch: five or\nsix more yards before the\ncorner, who bailed deep, arrives."]
SF_MOMENTS = [(0.0, "", SF_NOTES[0]), (1.3, "the throw", SF_NOTES[1]),
              (round(SF_CATCH, 1), "the catch", SF_NOTES[2]), (round(SF_CATCH, 1) + 1.0, "", SF_NOTES[3])]


def sf_after(fld, p, t, i):
    if i == 0:
        say(fld, p, 8.2, -10.8, "slant?", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, 2.4, -15.6, "flat?", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")


animation_or_strip(sf, SF_MOMENTS, lateral=(-19.5, 6.0), window=(-7.5, 15.0),
                   rings=(("HB", GREEN), ("WILL", GREEN)), after=sf_after)
```

Notice when the ball leaves: on the third step, before the halfback has even reached the flat. The
quarterback isn't waiting to see the halfback open; he's reading one defender, the Will, and throwing to
a spot the halfback will reach. That's what *timing* buys. The defense gets no time to react to the
throw, because the throw is already in the air when the receiver arrives. And it's what timing costs:
if the halfback is a step late because a linebacker bumped him, or the quarterback's third step lands a
beat slow, the whole thing falls apart. (The same concept from a modern shotgun spread, with a slot
receiver instead of a back in the flat, is in [The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd).)

Slant-flat is the play everyone remembers, but most of the 49ers' passing yards came from deeper: the
five-step drop, thrown on time to receivers crossing at 8 to 15 yards, with a back underneath as the
safety valve. The West Coast version of [drive](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-drive-concept) in
@fig-wco-drive shows the shape: a shallow cross under a dig from the same side, a high-low read of the
middle linebacker, and both backs as the last two reads, one on each side.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wco-drive
#| fig-cap: "Drive from split backs, West Coast style (illustrative, 1980s 4-3, Cover 3). The tight end (Y) runs a shallow cross at about 3 to 4 yards; the flanker (Z) runs a 12-yard dig behind him on the same line. The Mike (M, ringed) can come up for the shallow or drop under the dig, not both, and the quarterback reads him on a five-step drop, high to low: (1) the dig, timed to the top of the drop, if the Mike comes up; (2) the shallow, still crossing a beat later, if he drops. Both backs check for a blitzer first: the halfback then swings left behind the line (3), the fullback releases to the right flat (4). X's go route takes the left cornerback deep, and the free safety has the deep middle. Every receiver is running when he catches the ball."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
dfn = [q.moved(w=14.5) if q.key == "RCB" else q for q in era_43("one")]     # outside leverage on Z
p = Play(split_backs(), dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
p.dropback(5.0)
pass_pro(p)
go_to(p, "Y", (4.0, -11.0), kind="route", via=[(2.2, 3.6), (3.4, -2.0)])          # shallow cross
go_to(p, "Z", (12.0, -4.0), kind="route", via=[(12.0, 12.8)])                     # 12-yard dig
p.route("X", r.go(14))
go_to(p, "HB", (-0.6, -8.4), kind="route", via=[(-3.8, -6.0)], delay=0.5)         # check, then swing (behind the line)
go_to(p, "FB", (1.6, 9.6), kind="route", via=[(-3.6, 5.4)], delay=0.5)            # check, then the flat
p.drop("MIKE", (7.6, 0.8))
p.drop("WILL", (6.6, -7.0))
p.drop("SAM", (6.6, 7.8))
p.drop("SS", (7.6, 11.6))
p.drop("LCB", (15.5, -13.0))
p.drop("RCB", (15.5, 14.0))
p.drop("FS", (16.0, 0.0))
p.highlight("MIKE")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-21.0, 18.0), window=(-8.5, 18.5), title=False)
ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15))
num(fld, p, 12.0, -1.6, 1)
num(fld, p, 2.4, -10.6, 2)
num(fld, p, -2.4, -9.6, 3)
num(fld, p, 0.4, 11.2, 4)
say(fld, p, 13.4, 9.0, "Z: dig at 12", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 2.1, -6.6, "Y: shallow", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
point_to(fld, p, (10.6, 4.0), (7.6, 0.8), "M: up or back?", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -7.2, 5.2, "5-step drop", fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

Compare it with the plate in [Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd),
drawn from a modern spread, and you'll notice two differences. The first is the **read order**. That
chapter reads drive low to high, shallow first, because against man coverage the shallow is open early or
not at all. Walsh's version is read high to low, because of the drop. On a five-step drop with a hitch,
the dig is timed to arrive just as the quarterback finishes his drop and hitches up, so it gets the first
look; the shallow keeps running across the field and is still available on the next hitch; the backs
come last. Dig on time, shallow late, back last. Both orders work, because the Mike still can't take
both routes; what changes is which one the timing favours.

The second difference is where the outlets come from.
In the spread they're receivers; in Walsh's version they're the two backs, who were also the
offense's protection a second earlier. That double duty is the West Coast offense in one picture: the
same eleven players doing two jobs, so the defense has to cover more men than it expected.

## Design goal 2: yards after the catch

Every one of these throws asks the receiver to keep running after he catches it. That's not a happy
accident; it's what the routes were built for. The slant catches the receiver moving across the field
at full speed. The shallow cross catches him running away from the defender who started across from
him. The flat route catches the back moving toward the sideline with the cornerback backpedaling away
from him, at least against Cover 3, where the corner is bailing to his deep third. (Against
[Cover 2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-2) the corner squats in the flat, so the flat throw is
the one being taken away, and the West Coast answer was to throw behind him instead: the curl, or a
corner route into the hole between the corner and his safety.) In each case the receiver is already in
motion when the ball arrives, and the nearest defenders are either behind him or moving the wrong way.

A run after the catch is worth more than it looks. On the slant in particular, the receiver catches the
ball in the gap between the underneath zone and the deep zone, the only defenders who can tackle him are
a step behind, and one missed tackle can turn seven yards into seventy. That's how the 49ers' short
offense produced long touchdowns.

It also explains the 49ers' roster. Walsh's best players were the ones who could turn a short catch
into a long gain:

- **Jerry Rice**, a first-round pick in 1985 out of Mississippi Valley State, who finished his career
  with more catches, receiving yards and touchdowns than anyone in NFL history (1,549, 22,895 and 208
  total touchdowns).[^ricecareer] His signature was the slant, caught in stride and taken the distance.
- **Roger Craig**, a second-round pick in 1983, a running back who was also one of the best receivers on
  the team. In 1985 he became the first player to run for 1,000 yards and catch passes for 1,000 more in
  the same season, and he led the league with 92 receptions.[^craig] A running back leading the NFL in
  catches is the West Coast offense's fingerprint in a single statistic. Many of those catches came on
  the back's [option route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-option-route): he runs straight at the
  linebacker covering him, reads which way the linebacker leans, and breaks the other way, in or out.
  The linebacker has to commit before the back does, and against a back as quick as Craig a wrong guess
  is a catch in open field.
- **Dwight Clark** and **Freddie Solomon**, who did most of the catching in the early 1980s, and later
  **John Taylor**, Rice's partner on the other side.

The yards after the catch also mean the offense isn't at the mercy of how far the quarterback can
throw. Montana, a third-round pick, wasn't known for arm strength; nor, before him, was Virgil Carter.
What both could do was put the ball in the right place at the right time, which leads to the third design
goal. (YAC as a statistic, and the modern version that measures it against what a typical receiver
would have gained, *YAC over expected*, belong to the
[Shanahan case study](12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd), which is where the 49ers' current offense
picks this thread back up.)

## Design goal 3: ball placement

If the receiver has to keep running, *where* the ball arrives matters as much as whether it arrives. A
pass thrown to the receiver's back hip makes him stop, turn and reach behind him, and by the time he's
turned upfield again the defender is on him. The same pass thrown a foot in front of him, at chest
height on his upfield shoulder, lets him catch it without breaking stride. Walsh coached quarterbacks to
throw to a *spot*, placed for the run after the catch and away from the nearest defender, and receivers
to finish their routes so the spot would be right. @fig-placement shows three versions of one slant,
and why only one of them is a good throw.

```{python}
#| label: fig-placement
#| fig-cap: "Ball placement on a slant (illustrative close-up of the offense's left side, seen from above). X (ringed) takes three hard steps, breaks inside and runs across the field; the dashed blue ring is where he is when the ball arrives, and the arrow through it is his direction of travel. The cornerback, who bailed at the snap, is trailing behind and outside him; the Will linebacker is inside and underneath. A: the right throw, a step in front of X on his line, in the open space between the two defenders. He catches it running, and the dashed arrow is his run after the catch. B: a throw behind him. He has to stop and reach back, and the trailing cornerback closes on him as he turns. C: a throw too far in front and inside. He has to lunge for it, and it leads him straight into the Will, who can hit him as it arrives or take the ball. A top-down picture can show only where the ball arrives, not how high: coaches want A at chest height."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
p = Play([O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q")],
         [D("LCB", "CB", 9.5, -15.5, "CB"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.4, -3.0, "W")], los=35, to_go=None)
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (4.0, 0), (8.4, -5.6)], speed=6.8)
go_to(p, "LCB", (8.6, -12.2), kind="path", speed=4.0)                       # trailing, behind and outside
go_to(p, "WILL", (5.2, -4.6), kind="path", speed=3.0)                       # inside and underneath
p.highlight("X")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-19.5, 0.5), window=(-2.5, 14.0), title=False)
ax = fld.ax
# X's position when the ball arrives, his direction of travel, and his run after the catch
catch = (6.6, -9.8)
px, py = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, *catch))
ax.add_patch(Circle((px, py), 0.8, fc="none", ec=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 1.4)), zorder=7))
xa, ya = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, 5.5, -11.2))
xb, yb = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, 7.3, -8.9))
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xa, ya), (xb, yb), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=style.OFFENSE,
                             lw=1.4, zorder=8))
x0, y0 = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, 8.6, -7.0))
x1, y1 = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, 12.0, -3.2))
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((x0, y0), (x1, y1), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=11, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK,
                             lw=1.8, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=6))


def ball(d, w, tag, col, dx=0.95, dy=0.35):
    bx, by = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, d, w))
    ax.add_patch(Ellipse((bx, by), 1.0, 0.62, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=12))
    ax.text(bx + dx, by + dy, tag, fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color=col, ha="center", va="center",
            zorder=13)


ball(8.0, -7.8, "A", GREEN, dx=-0.95)
ball(5.6, -11.0, "B", style.DEFENSE_DARK, dx=-0.95)
ball(6.2, -5.6, "C", style.DEFENSE_DARK, dx=0.95)
point_to(fld, p, (12.0, -12.6), (8.0, -7.8), "A: in front, on his line,\nbetween the defenders:\ncaught in stride",
         color=GREEN, fontsize=6.9, shrink=9)
point_to(fld, p, (1.6, -9.4), (5.6, -11.0), "B: behind him: he stops,\nthe corner closes",
         color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.9, shrink=9)
point_to(fld, p, (1.8, -3.4), (6.2, -5.6), "C: too far inside:\ninto the Will", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.9, shrink=9)
say(fld, p, 12.4, -2.6, "run after\nthe catch", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.9)
plt.show()
```

The difference between A and B is perhaps a yard and a quarter of a second, and it is the difference
between the play Walsh designed and a two-yard gain. That's why the West Coast offense has a reputation
for chewing up quarterbacks who aren't accurate: the plays are easy to draw and hard to execute, and
everything depends on a throw that has to be right every time. It's also why its coaches have so often
preferred an accurate quarterback with an average arm to the reverse. The cost of that preference shows
up against defenses that crowd the short area and dare the quarterback to beat them deep.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, a pass is complete or it isn't; the receiver catches it and runs. In real life, a
"completion" covers everything from a catch in stride with open grass ahead to a lunge at a ball thrown
behind a receiver who is tackled where he lands. Box scores count them the same, and coaches don't.
When you watch replays, look past *caught or not* to *where on the receiver's body the ball arrived*,
and whether he had to slow down to catch it.
:::

## Scripting and practice: taking the guesswork out

Walsh is remembered for one planning habit above all: before every game he scripted his first fifteen
or so offensive plays (sometimes as many as 25) and called them in order.[^script] How a modern staff
builds and uses an opening script, and whether scripted plays actually gain more, is the subject of
[The Game Plan](../08-the-chess-match/08-03-game-planning-week.qmd); here the question is *why it
mattered so much to this offense in particular*.

A timing offense can't improvise its way out of trouble. A run-first team that has a bad week of
practice can still line up and run its best play harder. A West Coast team whose quarterback and
receivers aren't in sync throws incompletions and interceptions. So Walsh treated the week as
rehearsal for decisions, not just for plays. The script moved the play-calling decisions from the noise
of the first quarter to the calm of the week, and it let the players rehearse the exact plays they'd
run first, in order, until they ran them without thinking. It also turned the opening drives into a
set of questions (how does this defense line up against split backs? what does it do when the flanker
goes in motion?) whose answers set up the rest of the game.

The practices were built the same way. A 1990 review of Walsh's book on building the 49ers describes a
plan in which he counted out the days of training camp and the season in advance, used four practice
formats (from a hard two-and-a-half-hour session to a light half-hour the day before a game), and never
scheduled two hard sessions in a row. Individual technique was drilled to the step, down to how many
steps the quarterback takes and when he looks for each receiver. Plays were repeated until they were
automatic, and answers to special situations ("third down and four at the goal line") were prepared in
advance rather than invented during a game. His stated goal was that players "take the field to learn
something each session," not just to have their toughness tested. He also coached the coaches, which
is the beginning of the tree at the end of this chapter.[^csm]

There's a direct line from that practice field to the play this chapter opened with. The 49ers didn't
draw up Sprint Right Option in the dirt with fifty-eight seconds left. They had run it, including its
second option, all season.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Scripting and rehearsal exist because **a precise offense is only as good as its worst repetition**.
Walsh's plays left no slack in the timing, so he took the slack out of everything else: the order of the
calls, the week's schedule, the footwork. The trade-off is flexibility. A script is a plan made before
the defense has shown its hand, and a coach who follows it too faithfully can call a play the defense
is already set to stop, which is why every script has exits for third down, the red zone and bad field
position.
:::

## Signature play: The Catch (1981 NFC Championship)

January 10, 1982, Candlestick Park. The winner would go to Super Bowl XVI. The Dallas Cowboys had been to
five Super Bowls in the previous eleven seasons; the 49ers hadn't been to one. Dallas cornerback Everson
Walls had intercepted Montana twice, and his fumble recovery late in the game set up the touchdown that
put Dallas ahead 27–21.

San Francisco got the ball at its own 11 with 4:54 left and all three timeouts. What happened next turned
this chapter's idea inside out. All day the 49ers had used the pass where a defense expected a run; now,
with Dallas expecting passes, they used the run. The Cowboys played pass defense, and Walsh **ran the
ball**: Lenvil Elliott, a backup running back,
carried on several plays, and Freddie Solomon gained 14 yards on a reverse. In between came short
throws to Solomon, Clark and the fullback Earl Cooper. A team famous for passing drove into field-goal
range mostly by doing what the defense didn't expect. By the time they reached the Dallas 6 on
third-and-3, with fifty-eight seconds left, the 49ers had used two timeouts and had one left.

Why third-and-*3*, not third-and-goal? Because the line to gain was short of the goal line. A new set of
downs gives the offense ten yards to gain, so a first down earned outside the 10 sets the line to gain
in front of the goal line; on this series it was at the Dallas 3. The 49ers needed three
yards for a first down, or six for the game. (Goal-to-go starts only when the line to gain would be at
or beyond the goal line; see [Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd).)

The call was **Sprint Right Option**; the full call in the 49ers' playbook is "Change Left Slot – Sprint
Right Option."[^call] Read it the way [Offensive Systems](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd)
taught you to read a West Coast call: the first half is the formation, the second is the play.
"Left Slot" names a formation with two receivers on one side, one of them in the slot; "Sprint Right"
is the quarterback's launch point, with the line and backs protecting for a quarterback running to his
right; "Option" names the pass pattern. We couldn't find "Change" defined in a source we could check.
Solomon actually lined up in the *right* slot, so it may have flipped the formation, but treat that as
a guess. The 49ers lined up in split backs with Solomon in the slot on the right and Clark wide outside
him. The design:

1. **Montana sprints right.** A sprint-out moves the whole passing game toward one sideline. The
   quarterback gets away from the middle of the rush and runs toward his receivers, and the throws get
   shorter and simpler, because he only has to read half the field.
2. **Solomon is the first option**, on a short out toward the right corner of the end zone. The 49ers had
   scored on this exact play, to Solomon, earlier in the game.
3. **Clark is the second option.** He releases inside, across the path of Solomon's defender, a
   [rub](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rub-route) that makes it harder to stay with Solomon, then
   runs across the end zone to the left, stops, and comes back to the right along the end line, where
   the quarterback, still moving right, will find him.

@fig-the-catch recreates it, with Dallas in a version of the
[Flex](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flex-defense), Tom Landry's 4-3 with two linemen set back
off the ball.[^flex]

```{python}
#| label: fig-the-catch
#| fig-cap: "The Catch, recreated (simulated, BDB-format tracking). The 49ers' backs and receivers follow contemporary accounts; the tight end's side, the Cowboys' alignment (a Flex-style 4-3, with two linemen set back off the ball) and the exact paths are illustrative, not traced from film. Third-and-3 at the Dallas 6, 58 seconds left: the orange line is the line to gain at the 3, the grey area is the end zone, the thick line at the top is the end line, and the right edge of the turf is the sideline. Freddie Solomon (88) is in the right slot and Dwight Clark (87) wide right. Montana (Q, ringed) sprints right. Clark (ringed) releases inside, across the path of Solomon's defender (the rub), while Solomon, the first option, breaks out at the goal line and slips. Clark runs across the end zone to the left, stops, and comes back to the right along the end line as Ed 'Too Tall' Jones (72) and two other Cowboys chase Montana to within a few yards of the sideline. Montana pump-fakes, then throws high to the back of the end zone, where only Clark can reach it, over Everson Walls (24). Faint lines are the paths of the quarterback, the two receivers and their defenders, and Jones."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
LOS_C = 104.0          # the Dallas 6: BDB x = 110 - 6, so the goal line is d = 6 and the end line d = 16
off = line() + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("HB", "RB", -5.0, -3.2, "H"), O("FB", "FB", -5.0, 3.2, "F"),
                O("Y", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "Y"), O("SOL", "WR", -1.5, 8.2, "88"), O("CLK", "WR", -0.7, 13.2, "87")]
# a Flex-style front: the end on the tight end's side and the opposite tackle set back off the ball
dfn = [D("DEL", "DE", 1.7, T("5", -1) - 0.4, "E"), D("DTL", "DT", 1.0, T("2i", -1), "T"),
       D("DTR", "DT", 1.7, T("3"), "T"), D("JONES", "DE", 1.0, T("5") + 0.3, "72"),
       D("LBL", "LB", 3.6, -4.2, "L"), D("LBM", "LB", 3.8, 0.6, "L"), D("LBR", "LB", 3.6, 5.0, "L"),
       D("WALLS", "CB", 3.6, 14.0, "24"), D("SS", "SS", 2.6, 6.6, "SS"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 4.0, -10.0, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 8.0, -1.0, "FS")]
CATCH_OFF, CATCH_DFN = off, dfn
catch = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS_C, ball_y="right", to_go=3)     # right hash: the right sideline is w = 23.6
SIDELINE_W = catch.ball_y                                       # BDB y = 0
# offense
go_to(catch, "QB", (-8.0, 19.4), kind="path", via=[(-4.6, 5.0), (-6.6, 11.0), (-7.6, 16.0)], speed=5.6)
for k, dw in zip(OL_KEYS, (0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.0, 1.2)):
    catch.block(k, pts=[(0.2, dw)])
catch.block("Y", pts=[(0.3, 0.4)])
go_to(catch, "FB", (-1.4, 7.0), kind="block", speed=4.0)
go_to(catch, "HB", (-3.6, 8.0), kind="block", via=[(-4.4, 3.0)], speed=4.0)
go_to(catch, "SOL", (6.8, 11.0), kind="route", via=[(5.6, 8.4)], speed=6.4)                 # the out... and the slip
go_to(catch, "CLK", (12.2, 4.4), kind="route", via=[(4.6, 12.6), (8.4, 8.0)], speed=7.0)     # inside, over Solomon's break
go_to(catch, "CLK", (14.8, 11.4), kind="route", via=[(14.3, 8.6)], delay=0.35, speed=5.4)   # back along the end line
# defense
go_to(catch, "WALLS", (9.8, 6.4), kind="path", via=[(6.8, 12.0)], delay=0.35, speed=4.6)   # trails Clark across
go_to(catch, "WALLS", (13.4, 9.6), kind="path", via=[(12.4, 7.4)], delay=0.3, speed=4.2)    # and back, underneath
go_to(catch, "SS", (5.2, 10.0), kind="path", via=[(4.4, 7.8)], delay=0.5, speed=4.4)        # rubbed, then jumps the out
go_to(catch, "JONES", (-6.2, 16.0), kind="rush", via=[(-2.4, 8.4)], delay=0.15, speed=5.0)
go_to(catch, "DTR", (-5.6, 13.8), kind="rush", via=[(-2.8, 6.0)], delay=0.2, speed=4.6)
go_to(catch, "LBM", (-4.4, 11.8), kind="rush", via=[(-0.8, 4.4)], delay=0.5, speed=4.6)
catch.rush("DEL", pts=[(-1.2, 0.6)], speed=2.2)
catch.rush("DTL", pts=[(-0.9, 0.4)], speed=2.0)
catch.drop("LBL", (7.6, -3.2))
catch.drop("LBR", (7.0, 4.8))
catch.drop("FS", (11.6, 1.0))
catch.drop("LCB", (9.0, -8.6))
T_THROW = 3.3
catch.pass_to("CLK", t=T_THROW)
T_CATCH = catch_time(tracking(catch), "CLK", T_THROW)

CATCH_MOMENTS = [
    (0.0, "", "Split backs: Solomon (88) in the slot, Clark\n(87) wide. Montana will sprint right:\nSolomon is option 1, Clark option 2."),
    (2.0, "after the rub", "Clark's trail crosses over Solomon's break:\nthe rub that Solomon's man (SS) had to work\nthrough. Solomon has slipped: option 1 is gone."),
    (T_THROW, "the throw", "Clark has crossed and come back along the\nend line. Montana, near the sideline, pump-\nfakes (Jones, 72, leaves his feet) and throws."),
    (round(T_CATCH, 1), "the catch", "High, where only Clark can reach it.\n49ers 27, Cowboys 27; the extra point\nwins it, 28–27."),
]
CATCH_LAT, CATCH_WIN = (-6.0, 25.0), (-9.5, 16.0)


def catch_after(fld, p, t, i):
    ax = fld.ax
    # the end line and the sideline, drawn heavy because the play is about both
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = (fld.xy(120.0, y) for y in (0.0, FIELD_W))
    ax.plot([float(xa), float(xb)], [float(ya), float(yb)], color=style.INK, lw=2.0, zorder=2)
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = (fld.xy(x, 0.0) for x in (p.los + CATCH_WIN[0], 120.0))
    ax.plot([float(xa), float(xb)], [float(ya), float(yb)], color=style.INK, lw=2.0, zorder=2)
    if i <= 0:
        say(fld, p, 11.0, -2.0, "end zone", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, 14.6, -2.0, "end line", color=style.INK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -6.4, 21.2, "side-\nline", color=style.INK, fontsize=6.4)
    if i == 1 or (i == -1 and 1.1 <= t <= 2.4):
        say(fld, p, 5.0, 13.6, "slip", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")


FIELD_W = 160 / 3
animation_or_strip(catch, CATCH_MOMENTS, lateral=CATCH_LAT, window=CATCH_WIN, ncols=2, width_in=6.2,
                   rings=(("QB", GREEN), ("CLK", GREEN)), after=catch_after, mark_r=0.72, note_h=0.7,
                   trails=("QB", "CLK", "SOL", "WALLS", "SS", "JONES"))
```

Look at the third panel. That's the moment that gets called luck, and it's the moment the design is
working. The first option is gone: Solomon has slipped, and the Cowboys have him covered anyway.
Montana is out of room, a few yards from the sideline with three defenders closing. A quarterback
without a plan has two bad choices. He can take the sack, which loses yards and a down. Or he can throw
the ball away, which is safe but gives up the down for nothing: fourth down, one play left to score.
Montana had a third choice because the play had one. He knew Clark would be coming back along the end
line, so he pump-faked to buy half a second, got Jones off his feet, and threw the ball where only a
6-foot-4 receiver jumping at the back of the end zone could catch it. That throw was as safe as a
throwaway, because if Clark couldn't reach it, it would land out of bounds: no interception, and fourth
down still to play. But unlike a throwaway, it could also score.

Was it a throwaway that happened to be caught? People have argued about it ever since, and Montana's
own description of the throw has varied over the years. Clark's answer never did: the route back along
the end line was a practised backup, and he knew where the ball would come. Both things can be
true. The *throw* was a quarterback under pressure putting the ball where nothing bad could happen; the
*route* that put Clark under it was in the playbook and on the practice schedule. That is the
practice-field argument of the last section in one snap.

The rest is history. Ray Wersching's extra point made it 28–27. Dallas still had 51 seconds and moved
to midfield, but Lawrence Pillers sacked Danny White, White fumbled, and the 49ers recovered. Two weeks
later they beat Cincinnati, the team Walsh had left, 26–21 in Super Bowl XVI.

::: {.callout-important title="Why the sprint-out exists"}
The sprint-out (the quarterback running toward one sideline at the snap, with the routes flowing the
same way) **trades half the field for simplicity and time**. The quarterback reads two or three receivers
on one side instead of five across the field; he throws on the run, closer to his receivers; and he moves
away from the rushers who started in the middle. Near the goal line, where the field is short and the
end zone has edges a ball can be thrown over, those trades are worth more. The costs are real too: the
whole back side of the field is gone, the throws are harder to make on the move, and a defense that
knows the sprint is coming can chase it, as Dallas did. The modern cousins of the sprint-out are the
[bootleg](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bootleg) and the moving-pocket throws you'll meet in
[Play-Action, Boots, and Screens](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd).
:::

## The dynasty, and the system that outlived its coach

The Catch started a run that lasted longer than Walsh did. The table lists the 49ers' Super Bowl seasons
of the next fourteen years.[^sbs]

| Season | Head coach | Regular season | Super Bowl |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1981 | Bill Walsh | 13–3 | XVI: beat Cincinnati 26–21 |
| 1984 | Bill Walsh | 15–1 | XIX: beat Miami 38–16 |
| 1988 | Bill Walsh | 10–6 | XXIII: beat Cincinnati 20–16 |
| 1989 | George Seifert | 14–2 | XXIV: beat Denver 55–10 |
| 1994 | George Seifert | 13–3 | XXIX: beat San Diego 49–26 |

Walsh retired after Super Bowl XXIII with a regular-season record of 92–59–1 and a 10–4 record in the
playoffs. His defensive coordinator, George Seifert, took over and won two more titles with the
same offense, the second with Steve Young at quarterback and Mike Shanahan as offensive coordinator. A
scheme that keeps winning after its inventor leaves is a scheme that was taught, not just called.

Walsh's last Super Bowl was already a family meeting. Cincinnati's head coach, Sam Wyche, had run the
49ers' passing game as Walsh's assistant from 1979 to 1982, took the system to the Bengals in 1984, and
made the no-huddle their everyday offense rather than a two-minute tool. Montana beat him with a
touchdown pass with 34 seconds left.[^wyche]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: 49ers 1984 season, Super Bowl XIX"}
January 20, 1985, Stanford Stadium. The 15–1 49ers against Dan Marino's Dolphins, who had just set
passing records. San Francisco won 38–16, Montana was the game's MVP, and Roger Craig scored three
touchdowns, two of them on catches, the first player to score three in a Super Bowl.[^sb19]

**What to notice:** the running back as a receiver. Watch Craig's routes out of the backfield: he isn't
the last resort when everyone else is covered, he's a planned target, often lined up against a
linebacker who can't run with him. Watch for him stemming straight at that linebacker and breaking away
from his leverage, in or out: the option route. A defense built to stop a two-back running team has the
wrong players on the field to cover two backs who run routes.

**Where to watch:** NFL Films made an episode of its *America's Game* series on each of the four Walsh-era
and Seifert-era title teams (1981, 1984, 1988 and 1989), first shown on NFL Network in 2006 and 2007, and
it's the easiest place to see this offense on film. Highlights of The Catch are on the NFL's official
channels.[^americas]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: 49ers 1989 season, Super Bowl XXIV"}
January 28, 1990, New Orleans: 49ers 55, Broncos 10, still the most lopsided Super Bowl ever played. Montana
threw five touchdown passes, then a Super Bowl record, three of them to Jerry Rice.[^sb24] It was
Seifert's first season as head coach.

**What to notice:** the same offense without its inventor. The routes, the timing and the reads are
Walsh's; the play-caller isn't. Watch how often the ball is out of Montana's hand before Denver's rush
arrives, and how often Rice and Taylor catch it in stride and keep going.
:::

## The data fingerprint

The 1980s 49ers predate the free play-by-play data this book uses
([nflverse](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nflverse), which starts in 1999 and which
[Part 13](../13-analytics-and-data/13-01-nflverse-in-python.qmd) teaches you to load), so their
fingerprint has to come from the season totals: an offense that completed passes at rates other teams
couldn't match, threw relatively few interceptions for how often it threw, and had a running back lead
the league in catches. Montana led the NFL in completion percentage five times (1980, 1981, 1985, 1987
and 1989), and his 1989 [passer rating](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-passer-rating) (the league's
traditional all-in-one passing grade, built from completion rate, yards, touchdowns and interceptions
per attempt), 112.4, was the highest any quarterback had posted in a season to that point.[^montana]

What *can* be measured is whether Walsh's central claim holds up today: that a short pass can do a run's
job, and do it better. @fig-fingerprint splits every early-down play in competitive games from 2023 to
2025 (we drop plays where the [win probability](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-win-probability), the
chance from the score and clock that the offense goes on to win, was below 10% or above 90%, so
blowouts and kneel-downs don't distort it; [Win Probability](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd)
builds the idea) by what the offense did, a designed run or a pass of a given depth, and measures each by
[success rate](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-success-rate) (the share of plays that left the offense
better off) and by [EPA](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-epa) per play.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fingerprint
#| fig-cap: "Walsh's claim, tested on modern data. Every first- and second-down snap with the win probability between 10% and 90% (no blowouts), 2023-2025 regular seasons. Left: success rate. Right: expected points added per play. Passes are grouped by how far the ball was thrown past the line (air yards), with incompletions and interceptions counted. A designed run (scrambles and kneels excluded) and a pass thrown behind the line (screens, swings) do almost exactly the same job. A pass thrown one to five yards past the line, the heart of the horizontal passing game, succeeds far more often than either, and the six-to-fifteen-yard throws of Walsh's five-step game more often still. The last bar puts the sacks and scrambles back in, which is the fair comparison for 'passing' as a whole. Data: nflverse play-by-play via nflreadpy; course calculation."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
style.apply()
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.6), sharey=True)
labels = list(TAB.index)
y = np.arange(len(labels))[::-1]
cols = [style.MUTED, style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[2], style.SERIES[0], style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[2],
        style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[2], style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE[2], style.INK_2]
for ax, col, fmt, lab in ((a1, "sr", "{:.0%}", "Success rate"), (a2, "epa", "{:+.2f}", "EPA per play")):
    vals = TAB[col].values
    ax.barh(y, vals, color=cols, height=0.62, zorder=3)
    ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.9, zorder=2)
    for yy, v in zip(y, vals):
        ax.text(v + (0.008 if col == "sr" else (0.012 if v >= 0 else -0.012)), yy, fmt.format(v),
                va="center", ha="left" if (v >= 0) else "right", fontsize=7.2, color=style.INK)
    ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=9)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
a1.set_xlim(0, 0.75)
a1.xaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
a2.set_xlim(-0.27, 0.62)
a2.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
a1.set_yticks(y)
a1.set_yticklabels([f"{lab}\n({int(n):,} plays)" for lab, n in zip(labels, TAB.n)], fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
a1.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
plt.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

Read the top three bars together. A designed run on an early down succeeded
`{python} f"{RUN_SR:.0%}"` of the time and gained `{python} f"{RUN_YDS:.1f}"` yards on average. A pass
thrown behind the line, a screen or a swing, succeeded `{python} f"{SCR.sr:.0%}"` of the time: the same
job, done about as well. A pass that travelled one to five yards in the air succeeded
`{python} f"{S15.sr:.0%}"` of the time, with incompletions counted as failures. That's Walsh's argument
in today's numbers: the short throw is a *better* run, more consistent and worth more expected points,
and about `{python} f"{YAC_SHORT:.0%}"` of the yards on those completions came after the catch.

Now read down. The best bar on the left belongs to throws of six to ten yards, which succeeded
`{python} f"{TAB.iloc[3].sr:.0%}"` of the time, and the 11-to-15-yard throws aren't far behind. That
band is where Walsh's five-step game lived: the digs, crossers and curls you saw in @fig-wco-drive,
thrown on time to a receiver on the move. The deep throws are worth the most per play but succeed less
than half the time and carry most of the interceptions. And the last bar is the honest reminder that
"passing" includes sacks and scrambles, which bring the average for every dropback back down: a short
throw isn't better than *passing*, it's better than *running*, which is the claim Walsh made.

That raises the analyst's obvious question. If the deep bars are worth the most per play, was Walsh's
short-first offense *wrong*? Three things to weigh. First, the bars are averages over plays that weren't
assigned at random: a quarterback throws deep when the coverage allows it, often because the short
throws have pulled defenders forward, so the deep bar takes credit for a look the short game helped
create. This chart shows association, not a controlled test. Second, the deep throw's average hides its
spread: it fails more than half the time, and an offense that lives on it lives with incompletions,
sacks while waiting for routes to develop, and interceptions. Third, Walsh's real competitor was the
run, and modern data agrees with him there emphatically. Where today's analytics would push him is on
the mix. Even with sacks and scrambles counted, an early-down dropback averaged
`{python} f"{TAB.iloc[-1].epa:+.2f}"` EPA against `{python} f"{TAB.loc['Designed run', 'epa']:+.2f}"` for
a designed run, so a modern Walsh would probably throw more often on first down, and more of those throws in the six-to-fifteen-yard
band his five-step game was built for. Whether his short game was optimal or just optimal *for a team
with a weak line in 1979* is a fair argument; it was certainly better than what it replaced.

The league has absorbed the lesson so completely that it no longer looks like a system. In these three
seasons `{python} f"{SHORT_SHARE:.0%}"` of early-down throws travelled five yards or less in the air, and
`{python} f"{BEHIND_SHARE:.0%}"` were thrown to a receiver at or behind the line. Every team in the league now runs some
of Walsh's offense, which is the subject of the coaching tree two sections down.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"Short passes are just safe passes."** The chart says something stronger and something weaker. Stronger:
on early downs, short passes beat runs on consistency, which is what an offense needs to stay ahead of
the chains. Weaker: a short pass is not automatically a *good* play. Its value comes from the defense
leaving room underneath, and a defense that sits on short throws can make them fail. And on third-and-8
a five-yard catch is a punt, however efficient it looks on first down; there the deeper throw is the
right one ([Third Down](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd)).
:::

## How opponents responded

A system that wins three Super Bowls gets studied, and defenses found four answers. Each attacked one
of the design goals.

**Hit the receivers, and the quarterback.** The timing depends on receivers reaching their spots on
time, and inside five yards contact is still legal, so the first answer was to jam receivers at the
line and knock them off schedule. The physical extreme was Bill Parcells's New York Giants, who beat the
49ers in the playoffs after the 1985 season (17–3) and the 1986 season (49–3), the second game remembered
for the hit by nose tackle Jim Burt that knocked Montana out of it.[^giants] One story credits Parcells with the
name "West Coast offense" itself, as a jab after the first of those wins; another traces it to a 1993
remark by quarterback Bernie Kosar, publicized in *Sports Illustrated*, in which the label meant the
Coryell family of offenses from San Diego and was then attached to Walsh's by mistake. Walsh disliked
it either way.[^name]
