**Rush with safe pressure.** A quick-throw offense beats an ordinary blitz by getting the ball out before
it arrives, so defenses invented pressure that didn't leave a hole behind it. The Cincinnati Bengals,
Walsh's Super Bowl opponent twice, made Dick LeBeau their defensive coordinator in 1984 and became the
home of the [zone blitz](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-blitz), which drops a lineman into the throwing lane of
a hot route while a linebacker rushes, and which the NFL's own history describes as built to stop the
West Coast timing game; the story is in
[Zone Blitzes](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd).[^lebeau]

**Keep everything in front, and tackle.** If the offense lives on yards after the catch, take away the
"after." The [Tampa 2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tampa-2) of the late 1990s and 2000s was built
on fast linebackers and corners who sat short, let the short throw be completed, and swarmed the catcher.
Its best-known coach, Tony Dungy, had been Dennis Green's defensive coordinator in Minnesota, and Green
was a Walsh assistant: the tree was learning to stop itself
([Cover 2 and Tampa 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd)).

**Learn the language.** The West Coast call is long and explicit, and once a few dozen coaches had learned
it, they all spoke it. The best-known payoff came in Super Bowl XXXVII, after the 2002 season, when Jon
Gruden's Tampa Bay Buccaneers beat the Oakland Raiders, the team he had coached the year before, 48–21.
Rich Gannon threw five interceptions, and Raiders players said afterwards that Oakland had kept much of
Gruden's terminology and that Tampa's defenders seemed to know what was coming. (Derrick Brooks
remembers it differently: Gruden played Gannon himself in practice, and "we didn't know what play they
was running, but we knew their personalities.")[^sb37]

Today's version of the answer is the [two-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high) safety shell of the 2020s, which takes away the deep throw
first and rallies to everything short. The West Coast descendants answered that in turn, with
under-center play-action and the outside-zone run game, which is where the
[Shanahan case study](12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd) begins.

## The coaching tree

A [**coaching tree**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-coaching-tree) is the family of coaches descended
from one head coach, traced through who worked on whose staff. A branch runs from a head coach or
coordinator to an assistant who later ran a staff of his own; because most coaches work for several
bosses, one coach can sit on several branches. Walsh's is usually called the largest in football. @fig-tree draws the
branches that run through his offensive assistants, and the two boxes underneath list the head coaches
who came out of it in the 2025 and 2026 seasons.

Why did one staff produce so many head coaches? Partly luck and winning, which gets assistants hired.
But Walsh also built a system that could be carried away. Everything was written down: the 1982 playbook
ran past 300 pages (the call for The Catch is on page 325), and he later co-wrote a coaching manual,
*Finding the Winning Edge*, on how to run a staff, a practice week and a passing game.[^manual] The plays
came with their reasons attached, as this chapter has shown: why this drop goes with that route, why
the back checks before he releases. And everything was scripted and rehearsed, so his assistants spent
their weeks planning and teaching the system, not just carrying it out; in the words of the 1990 review
quoted earlier, he "coached the coaches." An assistant who leaves with a written, explained, rehearsed system can install it
somewhere else. One who leaves with a feel for his boss's play calls can't.

```{python}
#| label: fig-tree
#| fig-cap: "The Walsh coaching tree: the branches through his offensive assistants (selected). A solid line means the coach on the right worked on the staff of the coach on the left, coloured by the first-generation branch it comes from: blue for Seifert (and through him Mike Shanahan), orange for Holmgren, green for Dennis Green, amber for Hackett, grey for Wyche. A grey dashed line marks an important second mentor; most coaches had several, and only a few are drawn. Years are NFL head-coaching tenures unless marked. Mike Shanahan is the link to the modern wide-zone family: he never worked for Walsh, but was George Seifert's offensive coordinator from 1992 to 1994. Sean McVay's first NFL job was on Jon Gruden's staff (dashed), but he learned his trade in Washington from 2010 to 2013 under Mike Shanahan (solid). † John Harbaugh coached special teams on Andy Reid's staff, not offense; he's here because he became a head coach out of it. The two boxes list the tree's NFL head coaches in the 2025 season and in the 2026 season, after a winter of moves (checked October 2026). Defensive coaches who came through these staffs (Mike Macdonald, Robert Saleh, DeMeco Ryans and others) are left off."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
# (key, name, line under the name, column, row); children sit level with or just below their parent
NODES = [
    ("walsh", "Bill Walsh", "49ers 1979–88", 0, 3.4),
    ("seifert", "George Seifert", "49ers 1989–96,\nPanthers 1999–2001", 1, 0.6),
    ("holmgren", "Mike Holmgren", "Packers 1992–98,\nSeahawks 1999–2008", 1, 3.0),
    ("green", "Dennis Green", "Vikings 1992–2001,\nCardinals 2004–06", 1, 5.0),
    ("hackett", "Paul Hackett", "49ers asst. 1983–85", 1, 6.3),
    ("wyche", "Sam Wyche", "Bengals 1984–91,\nBuccaneers 1992–95", 1, 7.5),
    ("mshan", "Mike Shanahan", "Raiders 1988–89;\nBroncos 1995–2008;\nWashington 2010–13", 2, 0.6),
    ("gruden", "Jon Gruden", "Raiders 1998–2001,\n2018–21; Bucs 2002–08", 2, 2.0),
    ("reid", "Andy Reid", "Eagles 1999–2012,\nChiefs 2013–", 2, 3.6),
    ("mariucci", "Steve Mariucci", "49ers 1997–2002,\nLions 2003–05", 2, 4.85),
    ("billick", "Brian Billick", "Ravens 1999–2007", 2, 6.0),
    ("mccarthy", "Mike McCarthy", "Packers 2006–18, Cowboys\n2020–24, Steelers 2026–", 2, 7.2),
    ("kyle", "Kyle Shanahan", "49ers 2017–", 3, 0.0),
    ("gkub", "Gary Kubiak", "Texans 2006–13,\nBroncos 2015–16", 3, 1.05),
    ("mcvay", "Sean McVay", "Rams 2017–", 3, 2.1),
    ("harbaugh", "John Harbaugh†", "Ravens 2008–25;\nGiants 2026–", 3, 3.3),
    ("pederson", "Doug Pederson", "Eagles 2016–20,\nJaguars 2022–24", 3, 4.35),
    ("childress", "Brad Childress", "Vikings 2006–10", 3, 5.4),
    ("nagy", "Matt Nagy", "Bears 2018–21", 3, 6.45),
    ("mlaf", "Matt LaFleur", "Packers 2019–", 4, 0.0),
    ("mcdaniel", "Mike McDaniel", "Dolphins 2022–25", 4, 0.95),
    ("milaf", "Mike LaFleur", "Cardinals 2026–", 4, 1.9),
    ("kkub", "Klint Kubiak", "Raiders 2026–", 4, 2.85),
    ("oconnell", "Kevin O'Connell", "Vikings 2022–", 4, 3.8),
    ("taylor", "Zac Taylor", "Bengals 2019–", 4, 4.75),
    ("coen", "Liam Coen", "Jaguars 2025–", 4, 5.7),
    ("stefanski", "Kevin Stefanski", "Browns 2020–25;\nFalcons 2026–", 4, 6.65),
]
EDGES = [("walsh", k) for k in ("seifert", "holmgren", "green", "hackett", "wyche")] + [
    ("seifert", "mshan"), ("holmgren", "gruden"), ("holmgren", "reid"), ("holmgren", "mariucci"),
    ("green", "billick"), ("hackett", "mccarthy"),
    ("mshan", "kyle"), ("mshan", "gkub"), ("mshan", "mcvay"), ("reid", "harbaugh"), ("reid", "pederson"),
    ("reid", "childress"), ("reid", "nagy"),
    ("kyle", "mlaf"), ("kyle", "mcdaniel"), ("kyle", "milaf"), ("gkub", "kkub"), ("mcvay", "oconnell"),
    ("mcvay", "taylor"), ("mcvay", "coen"), ("childress", "stefanski")]
SECOND = [("gruden", "kyle"), ("gruden", "mcvay")]
HC25 = ["Andy Reid (KC)", "Kyle Shanahan (SF)", "Sean McVay (LAR)", "Matt LaFleur (GB)", "Kevin O'Connell (MIN)",
        "Zac Taylor (CIN)", "Liam Coen (JAX)", "John Harbaugh (BAL)", "Mike McDaniel (MIA)", "Kevin Stefanski (CLE)"]
HC26 = ["Andy Reid (KC)", "Kyle Shanahan (SF)", "Sean McVay (LAR)", "Matt LaFleur (GB)", "Kevin O'Connell (MIN)",
        "Zac Taylor (CIN)", "Liam Coen (JAX)", "John Harbaugh (NYG)", "Kevin Stefanski (ATL)",
        "Mike McCarthy (PIT)", "Klint Kubiak (LV)", "Mike LaFleur (ARI)"]

W, H = 6.6, 7.1
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(W, H))
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
ax.set_xlim(0, W); ax.set_ylim(0, H); ax.axis("off")
COLX = [0.04, 1.26, 2.6, 3.92, 5.4]          # the widest gap is the last, where four parents' lines fan out
BOX_W, BOX_H = 1.1, 0.42
TOP = H - 0.42
ROW = 0.55
GEN = ["Head coach", "His assistants", "Next generation", "Third generation", "Fourth generation"]
for x, g in zip(COLX, GEN):
    ax.text(x + BOX_W / 2, H - 0.16, g, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.4, color=style.INK_2, fontweight="bold")
pos = {}
for key, name, sub, c, rr in NODES:
    x, y = COLX[c], TOP - rr * ROW - BOX_H
    pos[key] = (x, y)
    root = key == "walsh"
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x, y), BOX_W, BOX_H, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.05",
                                fc=style.OFFENSE_TINT if root else style.SURFACE,
                                ec=style.OFFENSE_DARK if root else style.BASELINE, lw=1.2 if root else 0.8,
                                zorder=3))
    ax.text(x + 0.05, y + BOX_H - 0.1, name, fontsize=6.9, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="center",
            zorder=4)
    ax.text(x + 0.05, y + (BOX_H - 0.17) / 2, sub, fontsize=5.4, color=style.INK_2, va="center", zorder=4,
            linespacing=1.0)


# colour each line by the first-generation branch it descends from
BRANCH = {"seifert": style.SERIES[0], "holmgren": style.SERIES[1], "green": style.SERIES[2],
          "hackett": style.SERIES[3], "wyche": style.MUTED}
PARENT = {b: a for a, b in EDGES}


def branch_col(k):
    while k in PARENT and PARENT[k] != "walsh":
        k = PARENT[k]
    return BRANCH.get(k, style.MUTED)


# each parent gets its own vertical trunk inside the gap; the highest parent's trunk is the rightmost, so a
# parent's lines never cross the trunk of a parent below it
COLN = {k: c for k, _, _, c, _ in NODES}
TRUNK = {}
for c in range(4):
    parents = sorted({a for a, _ in EDGES + SECOND if COLN[a] == c}, key=lambda k: -pos[k][1])
    gap0, gap1 = COLX[c] + BOX_W, COLX[c + 1]
    for j, k in enumerate(parents):
        TRUNK[k] = gap0 + (gap1 - gap0) * (0.5 if len(parents) == 1 else 0.8 - 0.6 * j / (len(parents) - 1))


def link(a, b, ls="-", col=None, lw=1.0, dy=0.0):
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = pos[a], pos[b]
    x0, y0 = xa + BOX_W, ya + BOX_H / 2 + dy
    x1, y1 = xb, yb + BOX_H / 2 + dy
    xm = TRUNK[a]
    ax.plot([x0, xm, xm, x1], [y0, y0, y1, y1], color=col or branch_col(b), lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=1,
            solid_joinstyle="round", dash_capstyle="butt")


for a, b in EDGES:
    link(a, b)
for a, b in SECOND:
    link(a, b, ls=(0, (2.2, 1.8)), col=style.MUTED, lw=0.9, dy=-0.11)

# the 2025 and 2026 boxes (neutral outlines: their colours mean nothing about branches)
by = 0.08
bh = 1.66
for i, (lab, names) in enumerate((("Head coaches from this tree, 2025 season", HC25),
                                  ("Head coaches from this tree, 2026 season", HC26))):
    bx = 0.08 + i * 3.28
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((bx, by), 3.12, bh, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.06",
                                fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, zorder=3))
    ax.text(bx + 0.1, by + bh - 0.17, f"{lab}: {len(names)} of 32", fontsize=7.3, fontweight="bold",
            color=style.INK, va="center")
    half = int(np.ceil(len(names) / 2))
    for j, n in enumerate(names):
        cx = bx + 0.12 + (j // half) * 1.52
        cy = by + bh - 0.43 - (j % half) * 0.215
        ax.text(cx, cy, "• " + n, fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, va="center")
plt.show()
```

Read it from left to right and three big branches stand out, with two smaller ones below them.

**Holmgren's branch** is the one that kept the name. Mike Holmgren coached Walsh's quarterbacks from
1986 to 1988 and was Seifert's offensive coordinator, then won Super Bowl XXXI with Brett Favre's Packers
(after the 1996 season). His Green Bay staffs produced Andy Reid, Jon Gruden and Steve Mariucci, and
Reid's staffs in Philadelphia produced so many head coaches (John Harbaugh, Doug Pederson, Brad
Childress, Matt Nagy, and others) that his branch is a tree of its own.[^tree] It is also the branch that
changed the most. Reid's Chiefs, covered in [their own case study](12-04-reid-chiefs.qmd), still speak
Walsh's language, but their offense has absorbed college spread concepts, run-pass options and a great
deal of improvisation.

**The Hackett branch** is the quiet one. Paul Hackett coached for Walsh from 1983 to 1985 and later
taught the system to a young quarterbacks coach, Mike McCarthy, at the University of Pittsburgh and then
in Kansas City; McCarthy won Super Bowl XLV with the Packers, coached the Cowboys from 2020 to 2024, and
in 2026 is the head coach in Pittsburgh.[^hackett] Two more short branches sit at the bottom of the
figure. Dennis Green's Vikings staff produced Brian Billick, his offensive coordinator from 1994 to 1998,
who won Super Bowl XXXV with the Ravens.[^billick] And Sam Wyche, as you saw, took the offense to
Cincinnati.

**The Shanahan branch** is the one that rules the league today, and it has the most interesting
connection: Mike Shanahan never worked for Walsh. He was Seifert's offensive coordinator from 1992 to
1994, the years Steve Young ran Walsh's offense, then took it to Denver, married it to the outside-zone
running game and bootlegs, and won two Super Bowls. One of them, Super Bowl XXXII after the 1997 season,
came against Holmgren's Packers, 31–24: two branches of one tree meeting for the title, nine years
after Walsh's and Wyche's teams did.[^sb32] Through his son Kyle, Gary Kubiak and Sean McVay, that branch
produced most of the play-callers of the 2020s. McVay's first NFL job was on Gruden's staff in Tampa in
2008, which is why the figure gives him a dashed line from Gruden, but he learned his trade in
Washington from 2010 to 2013, as a tight ends coach under Mike Shanahan with Kyle as offensive
coordinator, which is why his solid line comes from Shanahan.[^mcvay] That family is the subject of the
[Shanahan case study](12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd).

**The 2025 and 2026 seasons, labelled separately.** In the 2025 season, ten of the league's 32 head
coaches came from these branches. The winter changed the list more than it shrank it. Mike McDaniel was
fired in Miami and became the Chargers' offensive coordinator; John Harbaugh, fired in Baltimore after 18
seasons, became the Giants' head coach; Kevin Stefanski moved from Cleveland to Atlanta. Three more coaches
from the tree became head coaches: Klint Kubiak, the 2025 Seattle offensive coordinator, in Las Vegas;
Mike LaFleur, the 2025 Rams offensive coordinator, in Arizona; and Mike McCarthy in Pittsburgh. In 2026
the tree has twelve head coaches. Super Bowl LX, after the 2025 season, was won by a Seattle staff with
both a defensive and an offensive root in the tree: head coach Mike Macdonald came up on Harbaugh's
Baltimore staff, and offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak from the Shanahan family.[^staffs]

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"Same tree, same offense."** A coaching tree records where coaches *learned*, not what they *run*.
Reid's 2025 Chiefs, Shanahan's 49ers and Harbaugh's Ravens share a common ancestor and almost nothing
on the field: shotgun spread and RPOs in Kansas City, under-center wide zone in San Francisco, and a
quarterback-run offense in Baltimore (and Harbaugh coached special teams on Reid's staff, not
offense).[^harbaugh] The data agrees. In 2025 the ten tree teams threw
`{python} f"{TREE_SH:.0%}"` of their early-down passes five yards or less in the air, the other 22 teams
`{python} f"{REST_SH:.0%}"`, which is no real difference, and Liam Coen's Jaguars, a McVay-branch team,
ranked `{python} ordinal(JAX_RANK)` of 32 in short early-down throws. What travels down a tree is a way of working (the explicit
language, the scripting, the attention to detail in practice) more than a playbook. Trees are also
generous: almost every coach worked for several bosses, and the drawer chooses the line.
:::

There's one more branch the figure can't draw. In the mid-1980s (1987, by the league's account) Walsh
began bringing minority coaches into the 49ers' training camp, to give them NFL experience and a
reference from an NFL staff at a time when the profession was almost entirely white. The league later
adopted the program for every team; it now carries his name as the Bill Walsh NFL Diversity Coaching
Fellowship. Dennis Green and Ray Rhodes, two of the first Black head coaches of the modern era, got
their NFL starts on Walsh's staffs. Herm Edwards was the first graduate of the program to become an
NFL head coach, and Marvin Lewis, Lovie Smith, Mike Tomlin and Raheem Morris followed.[^fellowship]
That might be the most important tree he planted.

## What survives

Forty-odd years later, almost nothing about the 1981 49ers looks modern: the split backs, the quarterback
under center on nearly every snap, the seven-step drop. And almost everything they *did* is still here.

- **The short pass as a run.** Every modern offense has a set of throws that does the running game's
  job: the [quick game](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quick-game), the
  [screen](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-screen), and the [RPO](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rpo),
  which goes one step further and lets the quarterback choose between the handoff and the throw after
  the snap ([RPOs](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd)). The fingerprint chart above is the league
  running Walsh's offense.
- **Backs as receivers.** Roger Craig's 1,000/1,000 season of 1985 was matched in 1999 by Marshall Faulk
  and in 2019 by Christian McCaffrey, then with Carolina, who was the 2025 Comeback Player of the Year in
  Kyle Shanahan's descendant of the same offense in San Francisco.[^cmc]
- **Timing and placement.** Quarterbacks are still taught to throw on rhythm, with their feet as the
  clock, and to put the ball where the receiver can keep running. The [Quarterback Play](../04-the-passing-game/04-07-quarterback-play.qmd)
  chapter is built on those ideas.
- **The script and the rehearsal.** Nearly every NFL play-caller scripts the opening plays, and every staff
  plans its practice week to the minute. Andy Reid's index card of first-and-second-down calls, in
  [The Game Plan](../08-the-chess-match/08-03-game-planning-week.qmd), is Walsh's script, one branch
  down.
- **The language.** The long, explicit West Coast call lives on in the Shanahan, McVay and Reid
  families. Jon Gruden's favourite, "Spider 2 Y Banana," reads like Sprint Right Option: a
  formation-and-protection piece ("Spider 2"), then one receiver and his route (the tight end, Y, runs
  the route the playbook calls "banana"), with the rest, including the fullback in the flat, left to the
  base pattern. Many staffs now shorten calls with wristbands and one-word names
  ([Offensive Systems](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd)).

What faded is mostly the *look*. The two-back pro set gave way to one back and three receivers, and
then to the shotgun; the fullback nearly disappeared (Shanahan's 49ers are an exception). But the look
is coming partly back: in 2025, offenses lined up with fewer than three wide receivers on 41.7% of plays,
the most since the NFL's tracking data began in 2016, and the quarterback was under center on about a
third of snaps, up from about 27% in 2023.[^trend] The descendants of Walsh's tree are leading that
return, for reasons the [Shanahan case study](12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd) explains.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: a West Coast census"}
Pick a team from the tree (the 49ers, Rams, Packers, Chiefs, Vikings, Bengals, Jaguars or any of the
others in the 2026 box) and chart its first-half first and second downs. For every pass, note two things:

- **Where was the ball caught, or where would it have been?** Behind the line, one to five yards past it,
  or deeper? Count the first two together as *short horizontal throws*.
- **Was the receiver running when he caught it?** If yes, how far did he go after the catch?

Then do the arithmetic. Across the league in 2025, `{python} f"{LG25:.0%}"` of early-down throws in
competitive games travelled five yards or less in the air; teams ranged from
`{python} f"{TEAM25.iloc[0]:.0%}"` (`{python} TEAM25.index[0]`) to `{python} f"{TEAM25.iloc[-1]:.0%}"`
(`{python} TEAM25.index[-1]`). A team well above the league figure is leaning on the horizontal game; a
team well below it is throwing downfield on early downs and running to set up its short game.

Don't expect a tree team to land high just because it's a tree team. In 2025 the tree's ten teams
averaged almost exactly what everyone else did (see the coaching-tree section): the short game is now
the whole league's, and what your count tells you is how *this* staff uses it this week.

**Post-snap, on the replay:** pick one short completion and watch the receiver's hands. Did the ball
arrive in front of him, at chest height, so he never slowed down (A in @fig-placement), or behind him?
And look for the backs: count how many times a running back releases into a route after checking for
a blitzer. That's the 1984 49ers, forty years on.
:::

```{=typst}
#set figure(placement: none)
```

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: eight in the box"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-box
#| fig-cap: "Predict the play 1. 1984, second-and-6 near midfield. The 49ers are in split backs. The defense has walked its strong safety (SS, ringed) down beside the linebackers, so eight defenders stand within about five yards of the line, with one deep safety and both cornerbacks 7 to 8 yards off the receivers."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
dfn = era_43("one")
dfn = [q.moved(d=4.2, w=8.8) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=8.0) if q.key in ("LCB", "RCB") else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(split_backs(), dfn, los=50, to_go=6)
p.highlight("SS")
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.0, lateral=(-18.5, 18.0), window=(-7.0, 15.5), title=False)
ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15))
say(fld, p, 8.0, 5.4, "SS walked down:\n8 in the box", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 10.6, 13.5, "corners 8 yards off", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 13.2, 5.4, "one deep safety", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

It's 1984 and you're calling plays for Walsh. Second-and-6 near midfield, split backs. The defense has
brought a safety down: eight men near the line, one deep, and the cornerbacks playing well off your
receivers. A 1970s offense runs here. What does the West Coast offense do, and where does the ball go?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**It throws, short and outside, and treats the throw as the run, to the weak side.** Count the box:
eight defenders against seven blockers (five linemen, the tight end and a back) means a run is blocked
one man short, and the defense built this alignment to stop it. But the same alignment leaves the edges
thin, and one edge thinner than the other. The strong safety walked down on the tight end's side, so
that flat now has the Sam *and* the safety in it. On the other side, the Will is the only underneath
defender over X and the halfback. So throw away from the rotation: the slant-flat to the weak side,
exactly the play in @fig-slant-flat-strip. The Will can't cover both, the corner is 8 yards off and
backing up, and the ball is out before the eight men crowded near the ball can get out to the edge.
Second-and-6 only needs the six.

This is the core of the chapter in one decision: the West Coast offense doesn't argue with eight in the
box, it throws the ball to where the box isn't. The defense's counter is to keep eight in the box *and*
press the corners, which leaves only one deep helper for the whole field; that's when Walsh went over
the top.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: press man against the backs"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-press
#| fig-cap: "Predict the play 2. A physical defense in man coverage. Both cornerbacks press X and Z at the line, the strong safety is on the tight end, and two linebackers (W and S, ringed) are assigned to the two backs (H and F, ringed). The Mike (M) has no man: he sits in the middle as a 'rat', looking for anyone crossing his zone. One free safety stays deep."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
dfn = era_43("one")
dfn = [q.moved(d=1.2, w=-13.0) if q.key == "LCB" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=1.2, w=13.0) if q.key == "RCB" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=3.4, w=6.6) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=4.2, w=-3.8) if q.key == "WILL" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=4.2, w=3.6) if q.key == "SAM" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=6.0, w=0.0) if q.key == "MIKE" else q for q in dfn]
dfn = [q.moved(d=14.0) if q.key == "FS" else q for q in dfn]
p = Play(split_backs(), dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
p.man("WILL", "HB"); p.man("SAM", "FB"); p.man("SS", "Y")
p.zone((7.0, 0.0), (4.0, 7.0), color=style.DEFENSE, label="")
p.highlight("HB", "FB", "WILL", "SAM")
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.0, lateral=(-18.5, 18.0), window=(-7.0, 15.5), title=False)
say(fld, p, 3.4, -13.0, "press", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 3.4, 13.0, "press", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(fld, p, (10.4, -6.6), (4.2, -3.8), "linebackers\non the backs", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(fld, p, (10.4, 6.6), (6.0, 0.0), "M: the 'rat',\nwaiting for crossers", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK,
         fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

You're Walsh, and the defense is built to break your timing: press the wide receivers so they can't
reach their spots on schedule, and hit everybody. Your receivers will be jammed at the line, and the
pressure will come fast. You have two ideas: a crossing route by X, to run him away from his press
corner, or a route for one of the backs. Which matchup is better, and what route do you give him?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The backs, on option routes.** Nobody can press a running back, because he starts five yards behind
the line. And the men assigned to them are linebackers, who are bigger and slower than a back like
Roger Craig. So give the back an [option route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-option-route): he
runs straight at his linebacker, and breaks in or out, whichever way the linebacker doesn't lean. (A
flat or swing that makes the linebacker run to the sideline, or an
[angle route](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-angle-route) that starts toward the flat and snaps back
inside, uses the same edge.)

The crossing route is the weaker idea here, and the defense drew it that way. Crossers are a good answer
to man coverage in general, but X has to beat a press corner first, which costs time, and then run
straight through the middle, where the Mike is sitting as a [rat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rat)
waiting for exactly that. The back's route stays outside the rat's area.

The trade-off is protection. If the backs run routes, they aren't blocking, and a defense playing press
man often blitzes. That's what the check-release is for: each back looks for his blitzer first and
releases only if nobody comes. Against a blitz the quarterback has to throw before the unblocked rusher
arrives, which is why the quick throw to the back, or the hot route, is the first thing he looks at.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: both options are gone"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-sprint
#| fig-cap: "Predict the play 3. Third-and-goal from the 6 (goal-to-go, so there's no line to gain: the goal line is the line), 45 seconds left, one timeout, trailing by 6. The offense has called a sprint-out right: the slot receiver Z runs an out as the first option (1), and the wide receiver X runs across the end zone and back along the end line as the second (2). The strong safety (ringed) has jumped the out, and the free safety (ringed) has drifted to the back right of the end zone and is sitting on the end line, right where X will come back. The quarterback is being chased toward the sideline."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
off3 = [q.moved(label={"SOL": "Z", "CLK": "X"}.get(q.key, q.label)) for q in CATCH_OFF]
dfn3 = [q.moved(label={"JONES": "E", "WALLS": "CB"}.get(q.key, q.label)) for q in CATCH_DFN]
p = Play(off3, dfn3, los=LOS_C, ball_y="right", to_go=None)
go_to(p, "QB", (-7.8, 18.0), kind="path", via=[(-4.6, 5.0), (-6.6, 11.0), (-7.6, 15.0)], speed=5.6)
go_to(p, "SOL", (6.8, 11.6), kind="route", via=[(5.6, 8.4)])
go_to(p, "CLK", (12.2, 4.4), kind="route", via=[(3.6, 12.2), (7.2, 8.4)])
go_to(p, "CLK", (14.6, 9.0), kind="route", via=[(14.3, 6.6)], delay=0.35)
go_to(p, "SS", (5.8, 10.6), kind="path", via=[(4.2, 9.0)])
go_to(p, "FS", (14.4, 12.6), kind="path")
go_to(p, "WALLS", (11.6, 6.4), kind="path", via=[(4.6, 11.4)])
go_to(p, "JONES", (-6.2, 15.4), kind="rush", via=[(-2.4, 8.4)])
p.highlight("SS", "FS")
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.2, lateral=(-11.0, 25.5), window=(-9.6, 16.0), title=False)
for xs_, ys_ in (((120.0, 120.0), (0.0, 160 / 3)), ((LOS_C - 10.0, 120.0), (0.0, 0.0))):   # end line, sideline
    (xa, ya), (xb, yb) = (fld.xy(x_, y_) for x_, y_ in zip(xs_, ys_))
    fld.ax.plot([float(xa), float(xb)], [float(ya), float(yb)], color=style.INK, lw=2.0, zorder=2)
num(fld, p, 7.8, 13.0, 1)
num(fld, p, 13.0, 7.6, 2)
say(fld, p, 4.0, 12.6, "jumped", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(fld, p, (11.0, 19.0), (14.4, 12.6), "sitting on\nthe end line", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, -9.0, 15.4, "chased", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 10.6, -6.0, "end zone", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
say(fld, p, 14.6, -6.0, "end line", color=style.INK, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

The same play as The Catch, on a different day, with one more thing gone wrong. The out to Z was jumped,
and the free safety has read the play and parked himself at the back of the end zone, exactly where X is
heading. It's third-and-goal from the 6, 45 seconds left, one timeout, and you're down by 6. Where
should the ball go, and what's the worst thing the quarterback can do?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Nowhere in the end zone: throw it away, out of bounds.** The second option worked in The Catch
because only one defender was near Clark, and the throw could go high, where only the receiver could
reach it. Here a second defender is already standing on the spot, facing the quarterback, so a high
throw to X is a jump ball with two defenders under it, or an interception. Both designed answers are
covered, so the right play is the one the design keeps in reserve: throw the ball over the back corner,
or over the sideline, where no one can catch it.

That isn't giving up. An incompletion stops the clock and brings up fourth-and-goal from the 6 with
about 40 seconds and a timeout left: one more full play, with a new call. The worst outcomes are the two
that take that play away. An interception ends the game. A sack is nearly as bad: it loses yards, makes
fourth down longer, and keeps the clock running, so the offense has to burn its last timeout just to
get one more snap. This is the other half of the lesson of The Catch. Montana's throw was placed so
that it could only be a touchdown or an incompletion; when the touchdown isn't there, take the
incompletion.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Walsh's problem was a team that couldn't yet run the ball, and his answer was to make the pass do
  the run's job.** The horizontal passing game uses short, timed throws to the edges and across the
  field, caught by receivers who are already running, so the ball beats the defense's pursuit and the
  tackle is made in space by a smaller man. Once it worked, the run came back: by 1981 the 49ers ran as
  often as the league did.
- **Timing, yards after the catch and ball placement were design goals, not happy accidents.** Drops
  matched route depths and the quarterback's feet ran his progression; routes caught receivers moving
  away from defenders; and the ball was thrown to the spot that let them keep running. The bill was an
  offense that needed an accurate quarterback and perfect rehearsal.
- **Scripting and Walsh's practice methods were the system's insurance.** A timing offense can't
  improvise, so he planned the week, the calls and the footwork in advance, and rehearsed even the
  backup options. The Catch was Sprint Right Option's *second* option, practised all season.
- **The data still backs him.** On early downs from 2023 to 2025, a pass thrown one to five yards past
  the line succeeded more often than a designed run, and a screen did about the same job as a run. The
  deeper throws are worth more per play, which says a modern Walsh would throw more, not less.
- **Defenses answered with press and physical play, the zone blitz, rally-and-tackle zones like Tampa 2,
  and by learning the language,** and today's two-high shells are the latest round.
- **The coaching tree is usually called the largest in football**: ten of the 32 head coaches in 2025 and twelve in
  2026 came from its branches. It grew because Walsh's system was written down, explained and rehearsed,
  so it could be carried away. What travels down it is a way of working more than a playbook: in 2025
  the tree's teams threw short no more often than anyone else.
